newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: GCA to seek advice on Australia's AWB restructure.
newsitem.headline: GCA to seek advice on Australia's AWB restructure.

text.p: The Grains Council of Australia (GCA) said it had agreed on transitional arrangements for the Australian Wheat Board's (AWB) privatisation by year 2001.
But GCA said it could not reach agreement on the allocation of shares in the new corporate entity which would replace the AWB, GCA acting president John Lush said in a statement.
GCA would seek a meeting with the Minister for Primary Industries and Energy John Anderson to request his counsel on the issue, Lush said.

GCA state affiliates had different options for the allocation of shares, ranging from one share to be issued to one grower through to one share issued for each 500 tonnes of wheat delivered, Lush said.
"The GCA is still confident that we will reach agreement on this pivotal issue," Lush said.

Lush, speaking after a GCA executive committee meeting in Melbourne, reaffirmed that the AWB would have seven grower elected directors, with two elected each by Western Australia (WA) and New South Wales (NSW) and one each by Victoria, South Australia and Queensland, one of which would be chairman.
When the current AWB board structure expired in October 1998, an election process would start on a state-by-state basis, he said.
This would be nationally coordinated for three A class directors, one each from NSW, WA and Victoria, and for one B class director, he said.
In October 1999, a further three A class directors, one each from SA, Queensland and NSW, would be elected, with one invited B class director to be selected by the new board, he said.
In October 2000, the final A class director from WA and a further B class director would be elected and the board would invite a further B class director, he said.

"This process will ensure that the new AWB has the range of skills and expertise to maximise returns to growers and also satisfy the financial institutions that will lend the AWB somewhere between A$3 billion and A$4 billion annually," Lush said.
Privatisation of the AWB would involve the issue of A class shares, which carry voting rights, to wheat growers.
B class shares, which would carry limited voting rights, also would be issued as part of a possible listing of the AWB on the Australian Stock Exchange.
